title: Enhancing Federated Domain Adaptation with Multi-Domain Prototype-Based Federated Fine-Tuning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to address the issue of data heterogeneity in Federated Domain Adaptation (FDA), which causes gradient update divergence in weight-averaging methods like FedAvg, leading to degraded in-domain and out-of-domain performance of the global model. Paper [6] explicitly addresses the problem of heterogeneous data domains in federated learning and proposes Federated Prototype Learning (FedPL) to enhance model generalization. Paper [8] also tackles domain shift in federated learning, focusing on adversarial domain adaptation to improve generalization across devices. Both papers share the same problem-class level objective of mitigating performance degradation caused by data heterogeneity in federated learning. Therefore, the purpose is **covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves uploading a proportion of domain-specific data embeddings (prototypes) from clients to the server, forming a prototype training set for supervised centralized training to obtain a global adapter, which is then distributed back to clients. Paper [6] uses prototypes (mean feature vectors) to address cross-domain performance gaps in federated learning, which is substantively equivalent to the proposed mechanism of leveraging prototypes for centralized training. Paper [21] introduces global prototype distillation for heterogeneous federated learning, which also involves prototype-based aggregation to improve performance. Both papers employ the same underlying primitive of prototype-based aggregation and training, making the mechanism **covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses DomainNet and PACS datasets with OpenCLIP pre-trained models, comparing against methods like FedAvg, FedProx, Ditto, MOON, FedProto, DBE, and local training. Paper [6] evaluates FedPL on DomainNet, which is the same benchmark family, and uses similar metrics for accuracy comparison. Paper [21] also evaluates prototype-based methods on heterogeneous federated learning using standard benchmarks and metrics. Since the evaluation design (benchmark family and metric semantics) is reused, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is Federated Learning (FL), specifically Federated Domain Adaptation (FDA) for image classification tasks. Paper [6] explicitly operates in the domain of FL/FDA for image classification, addressing heterogeneous data domains. Paper [8] also works in FL/FDA, focusing on domain adaptation across distributed devices. Both papers share the same general application area, making the domain **covered**.

## Purpose

The purpose is to solve federated domain adaptation (FDA) where data heterogeneity causes gradient divergence in weight-averaging aggregation (like FedAvg), degrading both in-domain and out-of-domain performance of the global model.

- Paper [8] "Federated Adversarial Domain Adaptation" directly addresses federated learning with domain shift across clients, aiming to improve generalization under domain shift in FL — this is substantively equivalent to the FDA problem.
- Paper [13] "Gradient Matching Federated Domain Adaptation for Brain Image Classification" explicitly addresses "domain shift across different sites may influence the performance of federated models" and proposes GM-FedDA — same objective.
- Paper [6] "Taming Cross-Domain Representation Variance in Federated Prototype Learning with Heterogeneous Data Domains" addresses FL with heterogeneous data domains and cross-domain performance gaps — same problem class.
- Paper [15] also addresses domain adaptation techniques in federated learning.

Papers [8], [13], and [6] all cover the purpose of addressing performance degradation due to domain heterogeneity in federated learning.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: clients upload data embeddings (prototypes = pretrained representations with domain-specific info) to the server, which forms a prototype training set and performs centralized supervised training to produce a global adapter, distributed back in one round with convergence guarantees.

- Paper [1] "FedPFT" transfers per-client parametric feature representations to the server for one-shot FL using foundation models — very close: clients send feature representations, server trains centrally, one round. The phrase "transferring per-client parametric feature" to server for centralized training is essentially the same primitive.
- Paper [6] uses "mean feature vectors as prototypes" shared to server for federated prototype learning — similar prototype sharing but aggregates prototypes differently (not centralized training on embeddings).
- Paper [21] "FedGPD" uses global prototype distillation where prototypes are shared — but distillation-based, not centralized training on uploaded embeddings.
- Paper [28] "One-Shot Federated Learning" uses ensemble/knowledge aggregation in one round — similar one-shot spirit but different mechanism.

Paper [1] is the closest: clients send feature embeddings (parametric features from foundation models) to server, server trains a global model centrally using those features, one-shot communication. This is substantively equivalent to MPFT's core primitive.

## Evaluation

The evaluation uses DomainNet and PACS datasets with OpenCLIP pretrained models (ViT-B-32/ConvNeXT-Base), comparing against FedAvg, FedProx, Ditto, MOON, FedProto, DBE, and local training baselines.

- Paper [6] evaluates on DomainNet with federated prototype learning methods — same benchmark family.
- Paper [8] evaluates federated domain adaptation on domain adaptation benchmarks.
- Paper [13] evaluates federated domain adaptation but on brain images.
- Paper [19] "Benchmarking Multi-Domain Active Learning on Image Classification" uses DomainNet as a benchmark.
- Paper [1] evaluates one-shot FL with foundation models comparing against FedAvg and similar baselines.

DomainNet is a named benchmark family used in papers [6] and [19]. The evaluation design (multi-domain image classification benchmark + FL baseline comparison) is covered by [6] which uses DomainNet in a federated heterogeneous domain setting with similar baselines.

## Domain

The domain is federated learning / federated domain adaptation / image classification.

- Paper [8] works in federated learning with domain adaptation for image/IoT data.
- Paper [13] works in federated domain adaptation for image classification (brain images).
- Paper [6] works in federated learning with heterogeneous data domains for image classification.
- Paper [1] works in federated learning with foundation models for image classification.

This is clearly covered by multiple papers.

### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to provide evaluation metrics that characterize the trade-off between knowledge retention (in-domain accuracy) and knowledge adaptation (out-of-domain accuracy) in federated domain adaptation (FDA). Paper [1] explicitly addresses the same purpose, as it benchmarks the trade-off between personalization (local adaptation) and robustness (global knowledge retention) in federated learning, which is substantively equivalent to the proposed purpose. The focus on understanding and navigating this trade-off aligns directly with the contribution's objective.

### Mechanism
The mechanism introduces new metrics, specifically domain knowledge retention loss \(L^P\) and domain knowledge adaptation loss \(L^A\), to evaluate the trade-off between in-domain and out-of-domain accuracy, along with radar chart analysis for fairness across domains. Paper [1] also evaluates the personalization vs. robustness trade-off in federated learning, but it does not introduce these specific metrics or a comparable mechanism for quantifying the trade-off. Similarly, while papers like [18] and [19] discuss balancing stability and plasticity in continual learning, they do not propose equivalent metrics or mechanisms for federated domain adaptation. Thus, the mechanism appears to be novel.

### Evaluation
The evaluation primarily involves defining the metrics and demonstrating their utility through empirical results, such as showing how different methods (e.g., local training, FedProto, DBE, FedProx, MPFT) perform on in-domain and out-of-domain tasks. Paper [1] uses a similar evaluation design, as it benchmarks methods for the personalization vs. robustness trade-off in federated learning, employing empirical comparisons across methods. This matches the evaluation design at the level of benchmarking trade-offs in federated learning, even if the specific metrics and methods differ. Therefore, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is federated domain adaptation (FDA) with a focus on evaluation metrics. Paper [1] operates in the same general area of federated learning, specifically addressing the trade-off between personalization and robustness, which aligns with the domain of this contribution. While the specific focus on evaluation metrics for FDA may be narrower, it does not constitute a genuinely new application area. Thus, the domain is covered.

**PURPOSE: 论证 MPFT 在降低计算/通信开销的同时保障隐私与对攻击的鲁棒性**

The purpose is to jointly demonstrate that a prototype-based federated learning method reduces computation/communication overhead while maintaining privacy and robustness against attacks. Paper [9] addresses "federated learning systems bottlenecked by communication costs" combined with DP, and paper [25] addresses "privacy and robustness issues" in FL simultaneously. Paper [7] explores "communication cost and data heterogeneity" with privacy in one-shot FL. However, none of these specifically target the combined objective of showing a prototype-based FL method achieves all three simultaneously (low overhead + privacy + attack robustness). Paper [9] comes closest by combining DP with communication constraints in FL, but doesn't address attack robustness. Paper [25] combines DP with Byzantine robustness but not communication efficiency via prototypes. The combination as a unified purpose is not cleanly covered, but at the problem-class level, paper [25] covers "privacy + robustness in FL" and paper [9] covers "privacy + communication efficiency in FL." Together these cover the purpose at the problem-class level — paper [25] is the closest single match.

**MECHANISM: (1) DP on prototypes; (2) prototype-based feature space hijacking attack; (3) compute/communication cost comparison**

For DP on prototypes: Paper [21] explicitly applies differential privacy to prototypes ("Differentially Private Prototypes for Imbalanced Transfer Learning"), which is substantively equivalent. Paper [2] applies FSHA to split learning with DP. For prototype-based feature space hijacking attack: Paper [2] explicitly describes "feature space hijacking attack (FSHA)" applied to a DP-enhanced learning system — this is the same attack primitive. Paper [13] also covers "feature space hijacking attacks" in split learning. For cost comparison: Paper [9] compares communication-reduction techniques in FL with DP. The mechanism of applying DP to prototypes is covered by [21]; FSHA is covered by [2] and [13].

**EVALUATION: Single-round communication overhead reduction; FSHA robustness under attacker with encoder + prototypes; DP noise trade-off analysis**

The evaluation design involves: (1) communication cost comparison across FL methods — covered by [9] which evaluates communication overhead in DP-FL; (2) robustness evaluation under feature space hijacking attack — paper [2] evaluates FSHA against DP-enhanced split learning, same evaluation design; (3) DP noise trade-off (performance vs. privacy) — covered by papers [3],[4],[16] which all evaluate the accuracy-privacy trade-off under varying DP noise. These evaluation designs all appear in prior work.

**DOMAIN: 联邦学习 / 隐私与安全**

Federated learning with privacy and security is the domain of numerous prior papers including [1],[2],[3],[4],[5],[6],[7],[9],[10],[12],[13],[19],[25],[28]. This is clearly covered.
